evidence_legend.strong: Consistent results from well-designed trials or major guidelines.
evidence_legend.moderate: Reasonable trials or well-understood physiology, with gaps.
evidence_legend.limited: Small or short studies, mixed results, or mostly mechanistic.
evidence_legend.practical: Working advice for sticking with the plan; not a research claim.

sections.title: Dietary
sections.lede: Built around two meals, a protein-first plate and a carb cap.

tips.title: Set protein by body weight, not by ounces
tips.summary: A daily target near 1.6 g per kg (about 0.7 g per lb) covers most people who lift, and it helps protect muscle while you lose fat.
how: Multiply your weight in kg by 1.6 (or your weight in lb by 0.73) for a daily gram target.
Split it across your two meals so each lands near half.
Log grams, not portions: a 6 oz cooked steak is roughly 45 g and six eggs are roughly 36 g.
tips.why: In a meta-analysis of resistance-training trials, gains in lean mass leveled off around 1.6 g per kg per day, with the upper end of the confidence range near 2.2. Eating far more added little for most people. On two meals a day, hitting the target takes deliberate planning.
tips.evidence_note: for lean mass alongside training; less direct for fat loss.
tips.caution: People with kidney disease should get a protein target from their doctor.
sources: Morton RW et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2018

tips.title: Eat protein and vegetables before the starchy part
tips.summary: Meal order can flatten the post-meal glucose rise, and it costs nothing.
how: Start with the protein and non-starchy vegetables.
Eat any starch or sweet item last.
Compare your rise for that meal in the Glucose section over several days.
tips.why: Small trials, mostly in people with type 2 diabetes, found lower post-meal glucose when vegetables and protein came before carbohydrate. Results in people without diabetes are less studied, so your own CGM curve is the better test.

tips.title: Cover electrolytes with food first
tips.summary: Headache, fatigue and cramps in the first weeks of low-carb eating are often about sodium, potassium and magnesium, and food covers most of it.
how: Salt your food to taste and drink broth.
Eat leafy greens, avocado, salmon and nuts for potassium and magnesium.
Drink water with meals, not only between them.
tips.why: Lower insulin makes the kidneys shed more sodium and water, so needs rise early on. The physiology is well understood, but controlled trials of electrolyte supplements for this are few.
tips.caution: Kidney disease, heart failure, and blood-pressure or diuretic medication change these rules. Ask your doctor before adding potassium or magnesium supplements.

tips.title: Count carbs one way, every day
tips.summary: A 50 g cap only means something if you measure it the same way each time.
how: Choose total carbs or net carbs (total minus fiber) and stick with it.
Log sauces, dairy, nuts and drinks; they are where the grams hide.
Enter the same number you would enter tomorrow, and adjust the cap in Settings, not the counting.
tips.why: Inconsistent counting turns the carb habit into noise, and trends in your weight and glucose become hard to read.

tips.title: Keep vegetables in the plan
tips.summary: A big salad or a plate of non-starchy vegetables keeps meals filling and the carb count low.
how: Make half the plate leafy or non-starchy vegetables at both meals.
Rotate greens, crucifers, and colorful vegetables through the week.
If digestion slows, add water and fiber-rich vegetables before anything else.
tips.why: Vegetables add volume, fiber and micronutrients for few carbohydrate grams, and fiber supports fullness and regularity.

tips.title: Test sweeteners against your own cravings
tips.summary: The research on non-sugar sweeteners and body weight is mixed, so treat the rule as an experiment, not a fact.
how: Go two weeks without them and note cravings, hunger and glucose.
Reintroduce one at a time and compare.
Keep what does not change how you eat.
tips.why: The protocol avoids sweeteners on the theory that they keep cravings alive. That is plausible but unproven for most people.

tips.title: Be careful with alcohol when little food is on board
tips.summary: Alcohol can lower blood glucose, mostly on an empty stomach, and it fragments sleep.
how: If you drink, do it inside the eating window, with a meal.
Skip it before hard training days.
Watch your CGM the first few times.
tips.why: Alcohol slows the liver's production of new glucose, which matters most when you have not eaten for hours. It also reduces sleep quality, which undercuts recovery.
tips.caution: If you take diabetes medication, ask your doctor first.

tips.title: Finish eating a few hours before bed
tips.summary: An early last meal suits sleep, and small trials hint at metabolic benefits.
how: Aim to close the window at least 2 to 3 hours before bed.
Use the Meal closed button so the tracker can see your real window.
If dinner runs late, shift the whole window earlier rather than skipping protein.
tips.why: Short trials of early time-restricted eating reported better insulin sensitivity, but samples are small and it is unclear how much is the timing versus eating less.

sections.title: Fitness
sections.lede: Strength first, walking after meals, intervals sparingly.

tips.title: Lift two to three times a week
tips.summary: Strength training is the most valuable habit on the list, because it protects muscle while you lose fat.
how: Cover legs, back, chest, shoulders and core across the week, in full-body or upper/lower sessions.
Do 2 to 4 sets of 6 to 12 reps per exercise, stopping 1 to 3 reps short of failure.
Rest 48 hours before training the same muscles hard again.
tips.why: US guidelines recommend muscle-strengthening activity at least 2 days a week. During a calorie deficit, resistance training plus enough protein is the main way to keep lean mass.
sources: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition, US Department of Health and Human Services, 2018

tips.title: Add reps, then add weight
tips.summary: Muscle keeps adapting only if the work gets slightly harder over time.
how: Pick a rep range such as 8 to 12 for each lift.
When you hit the top of the range on every set, add the smallest available weight.
Write your lifts down; memory is unreliable.
tips.why: Gradual increases in load are the core principle of resistance training. This double progression scheme is one simple way to apply it.

tips.title: Walk for about 10 minutes after meals
tips.summary: A short walk after eating blunts the post-meal glucose rise, and you can see it on your own curve.
how: Start within about 5 to 15 minutes of finishing.
Keep it easy; a conversation pace is fine.
Prioritize the larger meal, usually dinner.
tips.why: In a crossover trial of 41 adults with type 2 diabetes, 10-minute walks after each meal lowered post-meal glucose about 12% more than one 30-minute walk at any time, with the biggest effect (about 22%) after the evening meal. The evidence is strongest in type 2 diabetes; it plausibly carries over, and your CGM is the better test.
tips.caution: If you have heart disease, ask your doctor about exercising right after eating.
sources: Reynolds AN, Mann JI, Williams S, Venn BJ, Diabetologia 2016;59(12):2572-2578

tips.title: Build an easy movement base
tips.summary: Steady, easy movement underpins everything else and is hard to overdo.
how: Measure your average daily steps for a week before changing anything.
Add about 1,000 steps a day every 1 to 2 weeks.
Work toward 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate activity, including walks.
tips.why: Guidelines set 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity per week for adults. Cohort studies show risk falling steeply at first and flattening around roughly 7,000 to 10,000 steps a day; that is association, not proof.
tips.evidence_note: for the weekly minutes; step targets are observational.
sources: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition, US Department of Health and Human Services, 2018

tips.title: One or two interval sessions a week is enough
tips.summary: Intervals build fitness in less time, and more is not better.
how: After a warm-up, do 4 to 6 rounds of 30 to 60 seconds hard, then 1 to 2 minutes easy.
Keep them a day apart from heavy leg lifting.
Stop the session if you feel lightheaded or unwell.
tips.why: Interval training raises cardiorespiratory fitness comparably to steady cardio in less time. Adding sessions tends to add fatigue faster than benefit.
tips.caution: With heart conditions or high blood pressure, ask your doctor before high-intensity work.

tips.title: Put hard sessions after your first meal if fasted feels bad
tips.summary: Easy walking fasted is fine; lifting and intervals often go better fed.
how: Keep fasted-morning activity easy.
Schedule lifting and intervals after the first meal.
If you feel dizzy or weak fasted, that is your answer.
tips.why: Studies that match calories and protein find little difference in fat loss between fasted and fed exercise, so let performance and comfort decide.

tips.title: Protect sleep and one full rest day
tips.summary: Gains and fat loss both depend on recovery.
how: Aim for 7 to 8 hours in a cool, dark room.
Take at least one full rest day a week.
When lifts stall or joints ache for two weeks, drop volume by about a third for a week.
tips.why: Poor sleep undermines recovery, appetite control and training quality. The deload timing is common practice rather than a tested rule.

tips.title: Know when to stop
tips.summary: Fasting plus low carbohydrate plus hard training can occasionally leave you weak, so know your stop signs.
how: Stop for chest pain, fainting, or severe dizziness, and get medical help if it does not settle.
Ease off for sharp joint pain.
If your CGM shows a low with symptoms, sit down, eat something with carbohydrate, and tell your doctor if it repeats.
tips.why: Training on an empty stomach with low electrolytes or low glucose can cause lightheadedness. Recognizing it early keeps a bad session from becoming an injury.
